result.summary: A run of short fragments from Hesiod's Catalogue of Women, mostly quoted by scholiasts. They touch on the Argonauts' route, Circe and the Sirens, Aeacus and the Myrmidons born from ants, Peleus and the wife of Acastus, and Peleus' marriage to the sea-goddess Thetis.

scenes.title: Geography of Argonauts, Circe, Sirens
scenes.summary: Scholiasts report Hesiod on the Argonauts' route, Circe's western island, the Sirens' island and Ogygia. They also note that Arete was Alcinous' sister.

scenes.title: Hippostratus and Periboea
scenes.summary: Hippostratus weds a woman, and seduces Periboea, whose father Hipponous sends her from Olenus to Oeneus with orders to kill her. Macareus is also placed at Olenus.
scenes.stakes: Periboea's life is threatened by her father's order.

scenes.title: Aeacus and the Myrmidons
scenes.summary: Lonely Aeacus gets a people when Zeus turns the island's ants into men and women. They are the first to build ships and use sails.

scenes.title: Peleus, Acastus and Thetis
scenes.summary: Hesiod told at length how Peleus was plotted against by Acastus, who hid the knife made by Hephaestus so Centaurs would kill Peleus. Thetis refused Zeus and was doomed to marry a mortal.
scenes.stakes: Peleus risks death from the Centaurs on Pelion.

scenes.title: Peleus' wedding and other fragments
scenes.summary: Peleus returns to Phthia and is praised for his marriage to a Nereid. Other fragments mention the shared feasts of gods and men and Polydora.

notable_quotes.reason: Memorable origin of the Myrmidons from ants.
Evokes the golden age when gods and mortals shared feasts.

analysis.text: The fragments show the Catalogue's interest in heroic genealogies and how mortal lines connect to gods.
These passages survive only through quotations by scholiasts and ancient authors, showing how later scholars used Hesiod for geography and myth.

legacy.text: The marriage of Peleus and Thetis, parents of Achilles, became a major subject of later Greek and Roman poetry, notably Catullus 64.

fun_facts.text: Fragment 58 comes from a papyrus of the 2nd century A.D. found at Strassburg.

language_notes.text: A scholiast is an ancient commentator whose marginal notes (scholia) on a text preserve fragments of lost works like this one.
"Our sea" means the Mediterranean; the claim is that the Argonauts sailed round by Ocean, then carried the ship overland from Libya.
Tyrrhenia is Etruria, western Italy; the island meant is Circe's Aeaea, placed in the western sea.
Hesperian means "western", from Hesperos, the evening star or west.
"Son of Cronos" is Zeus (Jove). The Sirens were bird-women whose song lured sailors to death, known from the Odyssey.
Ogygia is Calypso's island in the Odyssey, where Ulysses was held; ancient writers disagreed about where it lay.
"Scion" means descendant; the Epeians were the people of Elis in the western Peloponnese.
"Far away from Hellas": Oeneus, king of Calydon, is imagined as remote, so Hipponous trusts him to punish his daughter.
The Myrmidons were Achilles' followers; their name was linked to the Greek word for ant (myrmex), which explains the story of ants becoming men.
"Father of men and gods" is a standard title for Zeus, who is called Zeus in other translations but appears here without his name.
Thwarts are the cross-benches across a ship where rowers sit; fitting them means building the vessel's interior.
"The very famous Lame One" is Hephaestus, the smith god, who was lame. The knife's divine making makes its loss more dangerous.
Iolcus was the city Peleus sacked, and Phthia his home region in Thessaly.
"Men who eat bread" is a Greek idiom for mortals, as opposed to the gods.

context_notes.text: Oeneus was king of Calydon and father of Meleager and Deianira; Althea was his first wife.
Olenus was a city in Achaea, on the northern Peloponnese coast; Diodorus cites Hesiod for its early settler Macareus.
Acastus' wife falsely accused Peleus of assault after he rejected her; Acastus then tried to have him killed on Mount Pelion, home of the Centaurs.
The Cypria was an early epic about events before the Trojan War. Thetis, a sea goddess, was fated to bear a son greater than his father.
Nereus was a sea god; his daughters, the Nereids, were sea nymphs. Thetis, Peleus' bride, was one, and she became mother of Achilles.

literary_notes.text: The claim that Sirens charmed even the winds exaggerates their song's power to show it overwhelms all nature.
Sails are called "the wings of a sea-going ship," imagining the ship as a bird skimming over the water.
Battle is compared to a feast, showing the Aeacids' eager joy in fighting.
The envious crowd's praise, with "thrice, yea, four times blessed," presents Peleus as a hero favoured by the gods.
